translation: Thomas L. Heath, The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements (Cambridge University Press, 1908). Public domain.
transcription: D. R. Wilkins, Trinity College Dublin.
note: Downloaded and parsed, not retyped. Propositions absent here fall back to the editorial summaries carried in the code, and every display of a statement reports which it is showing.

statements.I.1: On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle.
statements.I.2: To place at a given point (as an extremity) a straight line equal to a given straight line.
statements.I.3: Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the less.
statements.I.4: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal angles subtend.
statements.I.5: In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal straight lines be produced further; the angles under the base will be equal to one another.
statements.I.6: If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles will also be equal to one another.
statements.I.7: Given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a point, there cannot be constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it.
statements.I.8: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal straight lines.
statements.I.9: To bisect a given rectilineal angle.
statements.I.10: To bisect a given finite straight line.
statements.I.11: To draw a straight line at right angles to a given straight line from a given point on it.
statements.I.12: To a given infinite straight line, from a given point which is not on it, to draw a perpendicular straight line.
statements.I.13: If a straight line set up on a straight line make angles, it will make either two right angles or angles equal to two right angles.
statements.I.14: If with any straight line, and at a point on it, two straight lines not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles, the two straight lines will be in a straight line with one another.
statements.I.15: If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another.
statements.I.16: In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles.
statements.I.17: In any triangle two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles.
statements.I.18: In any triangle the greater side subtends the greater angle.
statements.I.19: In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.
statements.I.20: In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one.
statements.I.21: If on one of the sides of a triangle, from its extremities, there be constructed two straight lines meeting within the triangle, the straight lines so constructed will be less than the remaining two sides of the triangle, but will contain a greater angle.
statements.I.22: Out of three straight lines, which are equal to three given straight lines, to construct a triangle: thus it is necessary that two of the straight lines taken together in any manner should be greater than the remaining one.
statements.I.23: On a given straight line and at a point on it to construct a rectilineal angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.
statements.I.24: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other, they will also have the base greater than the base.
statements.I.25: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the base greater than the base, they will also have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other.
statements.I.26: If two triangles have the two angles equal to two angles respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely, either the side adjoining the equal angles, or that subtending one of the equal angles, they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides and the remaining angle to the remaining angle.
statements.I.27: If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the alternate angles equal to one another, the straight lines will be parallel to one another.
statements.I.28: If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, or the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles, the straight lines will be parallel to one another.
statements.I.29: A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles.
statements.I.30: Straight lines parallel to the same straight line are also parallel to one another.
statements.I.31: Through a given point to draw a straight line parallel to a given straight line.
statements.I.32: In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles, and the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two right angles.
statements.I.33: The straight lines joining equal and parallel straight lines (at the extremities which are) in the same directions (respectively) are themselves also equal and parallel.
statements.I.34: In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas.
statements.I.35: Parallelograms which are one the same base and in the same parallels are equal to one another.
statements.I.36: Parallelograms which are on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal to one another.
statements.I.37: Triangles which are on the same base and in the same parallels are equal to one another.
statements.I.38: Triangles which are on equal bases and in the same parallels are equal to one another.
statements.I.39: Equal triangles which are on the same base and on the same side are also in the same parallels.
statements.I.40: Equal triangles which are on equal bases and on the same side are also in the same parallels.
statements.I.41: If a parallelogram have the same base with a triangle and be in the same parallels, the parallelogram is double of the triangle.
statements.I.42: To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given triangle.
statements.I.43: In any parallelogram the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter are equal to one another.
statements.I.44: To a given straight line to apply, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given triangle.
statements.I.45: To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure.
statements.I.46: On a given straight line to describe a square.
statements.I.47: In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle.
statements.I.48: If in a triangle the square on one of the sides be equal to the squares on the remaining two sides of the triangle, the angle contained by the remaining two sides of the triangle is right.
statements.II.1: If there be two straight lines, and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangle contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments.
statements.II.2: If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and both of the segments is equal to the square on the whole.
statements.II.3: If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment.
statements.II.4: If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole is equal to the squares on the segments and twice the rectangle contained by the segments.
statements.II.5: If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half.
statements.II.6: If a straight line be bisected and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line and the added straight line together with the square on the half is equal to the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line.
statements.II.7: If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole and that on one of the segments both together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole and the said segment and the square on the remaining segment.
statements.II.8: If a straight line be cut at random, four times the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments together with the square on the remaining segment is equal to the square described on the whole and the aforesaid segment as on one straight line.
statements.II.9: If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the squares on the unequal segments of the whole are double of the square on the half and of the square on the straight line between the points of section.
statements.II.10: If a straight line be bisected, and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the square on the whole with the added straight line and the square on the added straight line both together are double of the square on the half and of the square described on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line as on one straight line.
statements.II.11: To cut a given straight line so that the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the square on the remaining segment.
statements.II.12: In obtuse-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, namely that on which the perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.
statements.II.13: In acute-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the acute angle is less than the squares on the sides containing the acute angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the acute angle, namely that on which the perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off within by the perpendicular towards the acute angle.
statements.II.14: To construct a square equal to a given rectilineal figure.
statements.III.1: To find the centre of a given circle.
statements.III.2: If on the circumference of a given circle two points be taken at random, the straight line joining the points wil fall within the circle.
statements.III.3: If in a circle a straight line through the centre bisect a straight line not through the centre, it also cuts it at right angles; and if it cut it at right angles, it also bisects it.
statements.III.4: If in a circle two straight lines cut one another which are not through the centre, they do not bisect one another.
statements.III.5: If two circles cut one another, they will not have the same centre.
statements.III.6: If two circles touch one another, they will not have the same centre.
statements.III.7: If on the diameter of a circle a point be taken which is not the centre of the circle, and from the point straight lines fall upon the circle, that will be greatest on which the centre is, the remainder of the same diameter will be least, and of the rest the nearer to the straight line through the centre is always greater than the more remote, and only two equal straight lines will fall from the point on the circle, one on each side of the least straight line.
statements.III.8: If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point straight lines be drawn through to the circle, one of which is through the centre and the others are drawn at random, then, of the straight lines which fall on the concave circumference, that through the centre is greatest, whil of the rest, the nearer to that through the centre is always greater than the more remote, but, of the straight lines falling on the convex circumference, that between the point and the diameter is least, while of the rest the nearer to the least is always less than the more remote, and only two equal straight lines will fall on the circle from the point, one on each side of the least.
statements.III.9: If a point be taken within a circle, and more than two equal straight lines fall from the point on the circle, the point taken is the centre of the circle.
statements.III.10: A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two.
statements.III.11: If two circles touch one another internally, and their centres be taken, the straight line joining their centres, if it be also produced, will fall on the point of contact of the circles.
statements.III.12: If two circles touch one another externally, the straight line joining their centres will pass through the point of contact.
statements.III.13: A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally.
statements.III.14: In a circle equal straight lines are equally distant from the centre, and those which are equally distant from the centre are equal to one another.
statements.III.15: Of straight lines in a circle the diameter is greatest, and of the rest the nearer to the centre is always greater than the more remote.
statements.III.16: The straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity will fall outside the circle, and into the space between the straight line and the circumference another straight line cannot be interposed; further the angle of the semicircle is greater, and the remaining angle less, than any acute rectilinear angle.
statements.III.17: From a given point to draw a straight line touching a given circle.
statements.III.18: If a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined will be perpendicular to the tangent.
statements.III.19: If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn.
statements.III.20: In a circle the angle at the centre is double of the angle at the circumference, when the angles have the same circumference as base.
statements.III.21: In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal to one another.
statements.III.22: The opposite angles of quadrilaterals in circles are equal to two right angles.
statements.III.23: On the same straight line there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of circles on the same side.
statements.III.24: Similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another.
statements.III.25: Given a segment of a circle, to describe the complete circle of which it is a segment.
statements.III.26: In equal circles equal angles stand on equal circumferences, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.
statements.III.27: In equal circles angles standing on equal circumferences are equal to one another, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.
statements.III.28: In equal circles equal straight lines cut off equal circumferences, the greater equal to the greater and the less to the less.
statements.III.29: In equal circles equal circumferences are subtended by equal straight lines.
statements.III.31: In a circle the angle in the semicircle is right, that in a greater segment less than a right angle, and that in a less segment greater than a right angle; and further the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle, and the angle of the less segment is less than a right angle.
statements.III.32: If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact there be drawn across, in the circle, a straight line cutting the circle, the angles which it makes with the tangent will be equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle.
statements.III.33: On a given straight line to describe a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to a given rectilinear angle.
statements.III.34: From a given circle to cut off a segment admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.
statements.III.35: If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.
statements.III.36: If a point be taken outside a circle and from it there fall on the circle two straight lines, and if one of them cut the circle and the other touch it, the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference will be equal to the square on the tangent.
statements.III.37: If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point there fall on the circle two straight lines, if one of them cut the circle, and the other fall on it, and if further the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference be equal to the square on the straight line which falls on the circle, the straight line which fall on it will touch the circle.
statements.IV.1: Into a given circle to fit a straight line equal to a given straight line which is not greater than the diameter of the circle.
statements.IV.2: In a given circle to inscribe a triangle equiangular with a given triangle.
statements.IV.3: About a given circle to circumscribe a triangle equiangular with a given triangle.
statements.IV.4: In a given triangle to inscribe a circle.
statements.IV.5: About a given triangle to circumscribe a circle.
statements.IV.6: In a given circle to inscribe a square.
statements.IV.7: About a given circle to circumscribe a square.
statements.IV.8: In a given square to inscribe a circle.
statements.IV.9: About a given square to circumscribe a circle.
statements.IV.10: To construct an isosceles triangle havng each of the angles at the base double of the remaining one.
statements.IV.11: In a given circle to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon.
statements.IV.12: About a given circle to circumscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon.
statements.IV.13: In a given pentagon, which is equilateral and equiangular, to inscribe a circle.
statements.IV.14: About a given pentagon, which is equilateral and equiangular, to circumscribe a circle.
statements.IV.15: In a given circle to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular hexagon.
statements.IV.16: In a given circle to inscribe a fifteen-angled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular.
